objectives: Secure a negotiated settlement with the UK that lets the EU conclude Council approval on schedule in June, avoiding an unresolved Article XXVIII lapsing into unilateral action and retaliation.

Preserve the substance of the EU's steel regime (50% out-of-quota rate, restrictive global TRQ) while making targeted concessions on volume, administration or carve-outs that are cheap for the EU but valuable to the UK.
Avoid setting a precedent of easy flexibility that Turkey, Korea, India or Japan could exploit in their parallel claims.
Prevent the UK from joining a coalition with Japan/Korea to retaliate against the FTA-disapplication clause specifically.
Protect the EU's institutional credibility in Geneva as a serious, firm negotiating partner for future Article XXVIII and safeguard actions.
Where possible, use the UK's own steel safeguard and its treatment of EU exporters as leverage/linkage to extract reciprocal restraint.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement (or credible near-settlement) by Round 4 that keeps the 50% bound rate and most of the TRQ architecture intact, with only marginal concessions (e.g. a modest country-specific share or review clause), no joint UK-Japan-Korea retaliation coalition forming, and the UK's own safeguard treatment of EU exporters left undisturbed or improved. Failure: EU forced into large volume/allocation concessions, UK walks away and triggers retaliation in concert with other claimants, or Brussels has to intervene to overrule the Geneva line because I've either conceded too much or caused a breakdown that threatens the June Council timeline.
declaration.approach: Open firm: defend the package as a coherent response to overcapacity, resist early movement on headline numbers (rate, volume, FCFS allocation) to avoid signalling weakness. Use Phase 2 consultations to genuinely probe the UK's real red lines (industry sites, product concentration) versus its opening asks, and feed Brussels an honest read of what minimal package could close this. Look for asymmetric trades — things costly to the UK to keep pushing but cheap for the EU to give (e.g. a review clause, licensing rather than pure FCFS to give the UK predictability, a carved-out product line where UK exposure is concentrated) — rather than moving on the headline rate or aggregate volume. Explicitly and early flag the linkage between the EU's FTA-disapplication clause and the UK's own safeguard treatment of EU exporters, to keep the negotiation bilateral and transactional rather than feeding a multilateral grievance with Japan/Korea. Hold back real flexibility until Round 3, use Round 1-2 to test resolve and gather information, and only move if the UK demonstrates it is prepared to settle rather than escalate.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Meaningful increase in tariff-free volume and/or a UK-specific country share (not pure global FCFS) reflecting historic trade levels; preservation of FTA-equivalent access under the TCA rather than being lumped in with third countries; protection for a concentrated set of product lines/sites with high employment sensitivity; a review clause or sunset; and reciprocal favourable treatment for EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard. They will want to show their industry and Parliament that they extracted real compensation, and will be tempted to coordinate with Japan/Korea if they feel unheard.

Their own generous country shares or carve-outs; they will be watching the EU-UK outcome as a benchmark and may press harder if the UK secures a strong deal, so the EU has an interest in not over-conceding to the UK precisely because of this read-across.

parties.who: Japan / Korea (as potential coalition partners with UK on FTA disapplication)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To use the UK's grievance over FTA disapplication as leverage to jointly contest that specific element, widening the dispute beyond bilateral EU-UK terms; the EU wants to defuse this by resolving the UK's core volume/allocation concerns bilaterally before this coalition solidifies.

A concluded process by June with Council able to vote on schedule; internal balance between steel-producing member states (want firmness) and steel-consuming/manufacturing member states (want a settlement that avoids retaliation and trade disruption); will expect me to hold the line on the core rate/volume architecture while giving me some room on administration/technical elements.

objectives: Secure UK agreement to the Article XXVIII modification within four rounds so the Council can vote in June

Preserve the integrity of the import regime: keep the 50% out-of-quota rate and overall TRQ volume close to 400,000t, resisting a country-specific UK carve-out that would fragment the global allocation
Avoid setting a precedent that other principal suppliers (Turkey, Korea) or FTA partners can point to for larger shares or better terms

Obtain something creditable to present to the Trade Policy Committee and Council as 'compensation' that member states with steel-consuming industries will not reject as too generous, and steel-producing member states will not reject as too weak
Manage the FTA disapplication issue so it doesn't get reopened as a UK veto point, while keeping flexibility on a modest preferential pool if it buys UK sign-off cheaply

Avoid triggering UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions against EU exporters into the UK, and avoid worsening EU exporters' position under the UK's own steel safeguard/quota allocations
Keep a review clause or duration limit as a fallback concession that costs little now but signals flexibility
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: UK accepts terms in Rounds 1-3 that keep the out-of-quota rate at or near 50%, keep the TRQ at or near 400,000t globally administered (or with only a modest, defensible UK-specific carve-out/sub-quota), and secure EU exporters at least standstill treatment under the UK's own safeguard, all concluded in time for June Council vote. Partial success: agreement reached in Round 4 with some erosion (e.g. slightly higher volume or a UK-specific tranche) but core architecture intact and no cascading claims from Turkey/Korea. Failure: no deal after Round 4, forcing the default 50%/400kt/global FCFS regime into force with no review clause, UK withdrawal of concessions damaging EU exporters, and a worse political and legal position for the Commission with the TPC and Council for having designed a regime that provoked WTO-consistent retaliation.
declaration.approach: Open firm on the core architecture (50% out-of-quota rate, ~400,000t global TRQ) as the anchor, framed as necessary given non-market-economy overcapacity and the parallel Turkey/Korea claims - conceding the headline rate or volume early invites those larger suppliers to demand the same. Offer movement on secondary, cheaper-to-concede dimensions first: administration method (licensing vs FCFS to give UK exporters more predictable access within the existing volume), duration and a review clause, and enforcement/circumvention provisions favourable to UK-origin steel. Use the FTA-disapplication and TCA interaction as a bargaining chip - signal willingness to soften disapplication or carve a modest UK-specific tranche within the global TRQ (not additional volume) in exchange for UK restraint on its own safeguard treatment of EU exporters and quick sign-off. Hold compensation elsewhere in the schedule as a last-resort sweetener rather than a first offer, since it's costly to sell to the TPC. Escalate concessions gradually across rounds, saving the more costly moves (e.g. a country-specific share or slight review clause with volume rebasing) for Round 3, to test UK resolve and give capital time to feel the pressure of a looming no-deal default. Coordinate closely between rounds with capital to ensure Council-sellable framing; avoid appearing to bid against myself.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum preservation of tariff-free access volume, ideally a UK-specific country share rather than global FCFS (which UK exporters could lose out on to faster-moving competitors), a lower or delayed out-of-quota rate, protection of the TCA relationship and reversal or softening of FTA disapplication, and reciprocal generous treatment for EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard. Will be under strong domestic pressure given concentrated employment impact, but also aware a no-deal scenario hurts UK industry more and delays certainty.

Watching the UK settlement closely as a benchmark; want equal or better treatment for their own volumes given Turkey and Korea ship more. Will not accept the UK getting a materially better rate or share without seeking the same.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (e.g. Italy, Germany, Spain, France)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum protection - want the 50% rate, TRQ volume, and FTA disapplication preserved or tightened; will resist any generous carve-out for the UK or expanded FTA preferential pool.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors (e.g. automotive, construction)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Want sufficient tariff-free volume and predictable administration to avoid input cost spikes; may push back if the regime is too restrictive or if UK-specific carve-outs create supply chain disruption.

Threatening retaliation against EU steel measures generally; increases Commission's incentive to conclude the UK negotiation quickly and cleanly to avoid multiple fronts, but doesn't directly want anything from this negotiation.

A politically presentable deal concluded on schedule for June Council vote, defensible as protecting EU steel industry from non-market-economy overcapacity while not appearing to have capitulated to the UK or provoked unnecessary retaliation.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK share of the TRQ (not global first-come-first-served) sized to protect the bulk of current UK export volumes at zero duty, ideally close to the 2.4mt three-year average rather than a share diluted by Turkey/Korea competition
Preserve or restore FTA-equivalent treatment for UK steel under the EU regime, or at minimum avoid the UK being singled out for disapplication relative to other FTA partners
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration so the TRQ isn't a permanent, unreviewable ratchet against UK industry
Extract compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule if volume/access asks cannot be fully met, to offset value lost
Avoid escalation into a mutual UK-EU tariff war given the EU is also the UK's largest steel import source and the UK has its own parallel safeguard/Art XXVIII process where EU holds quota
Keep the UK's own steel safeguard/TRQ process on a track that doesn't get hijacked or used as leverage against us, and manage EU expectations on reciprocal treatment there
Avoid being drawn into a joint Japan/Korea retaliation front that could complicate or slow the bilateral EU-UK settlement or create obligations London hasn't sanctioned
Gather clear, reportable intelligence for London on the EU's real floor/ceiling before capital has to decide on a settlement figure it hasn't yet given me
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settled outcome (within four rounds) that secures a UK-specific quota share materially protecting current export volumes, some form of review/duration limit, and either restored FTA-consistent treatment or clear compensation offsetting its loss — reached without triggering a wider retaliatory spiral with the EU that damages the UK-EU steel relationship or the TCA. Partial success: no deal but a clearly mapped EU floor, UK preserving its right to retaliate proportionately and in a form that protects UK industry rather than just symbolically hurting EU exporters. Failure: global FCFS quota stands unchanged, no UK-specific protection, no compensation, and/or the UK gets drawn into an uncoordinated multilateral retaliation bloc that removes flexibility from London or damages the TCA relationship without commensurate gain for UK steel.
declaration.approach: Move early to test whether the EU's opening position is genuinely their floor or a negotiating anchor before the June Council deadline forces movement. Use the timeline pressure on the Commission (Council vote in June) as leverage — they need a deal or a clean unilateral notification, and an unresolved UK claim complicates their domestic legislative process since they've explicitly tied the TRQ design to this negotiation. Prioritise volume/allocation method (country share) over headline bound rate, since a workable quota share is what actually protects industry; treat the out-of-quota 50% rate as less urgent if in-quota access is adequate. Keep tone technical and constructive at the table — I'll be dealing with this counterpart on other Goods files after this concludes, so avoid personalising conflict. Report faithfully to London each round what the EU actually offers versus their opening position, flag the gap versus what would protect industry, and push capital for an actual settlement range rather than operating blind. Resist Japan/Korea's push for a joint retaliatory front for now — note it as leverage in reserve, keep it in play as a signal to the EU that non-settlement has multilateral costs, but don't commit the UK to coordinated action without London's explicit sign-off, since our own parallel safeguard process gives us independent leverage that a joint bloc might dilute or complicate.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A deal that lets them close this by June with minimal reopening of the domestic TRQ legislation, protection for EU steel producers from perceived circumvention via UK-origin or transshipped non-market-economy steel, and to avoid setting a precedent that invites similar demands from Turkey/Korea/India/Japan; likely willing to move on UK-specific share or review clause but resistant to reopening the headline rate or global-FCFS structure wholesale

Protection of UK steel jobs and output, political cover of 'standing firm' against a damaging EU measure, but also awareness that no-deal retaliation takes 6+ months and doesn't fix market access now; will want regular reporting and likely to be cautious about authorising retaliation that hits EU exporters given UK's own reliance on EU steel imports

To recruit the UK into a joint FTA-disapplication retaliation or coordinated pressure campaign against the EU, using UK grievance over FTA carve-out as the wedge; their interest is in maximising pressure on the EU generally, not necessarily aligned with UK's specific need for a country quota share

parties.who: Turkey / Korea (as principal suppliers, separate track)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own larger-volume country shares of the TRQ; their claims will shape how much globally-allocated volume is 'left' for the UK if allocation stays global, so their parallel negotiation indirectly competes with UK's ask

Producer states (e.g. steel-producing members) want the tightest possible measure; consuming-industry states want more liberal quota; this internal split may give the Commission limited room to move and explains urgency to lock in Council approval by June

objectives: Secure a UK-specific quota share (carved out from or ring-fenced within the global TRQ) sized against our recent trade volumes (~2.4Mt/yr), not a first-come-first-served free-for-all where Turkey and Korea's larger volumes crowd us out
Push the TRQ volume up from 400,000t and/or secure product-line carve-outs for the narrower range of products the UK is concentrated in

Prevent the disapplication of FTA/TCA tariff treatment from applying to the UK specifically - argue the UK should be treated at least as well as other FTA partners, ideally with TCA-specific preferential access preserved
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration so this isn't a permanent settlement of a temporary problem
Get meaningful compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule if the steel terms themselves can't be improved enough
Preserve leverage on our own UK safeguard - only offer improved EU country-specific allocations there in exchange for real, substantial EU concessions here
Avoid a scenario where UK steel producers conclude the deal is too poor to justify further investment, triggering plant closures
Keep open the credible threat of withdrawing equivalent concessions if no deal, without actually wanting to use it (six-month delay, retaliation hits UK importers of EU steel too)
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a UK-specific quota share meaningfully above our pro-rata share of the global 400kt (or a larger global volume with FCFS administration structured so UK exporters can realistically access it), no blanket FTA-disapplication targeting UK, a review clause within 2-3 years, and/or compensation elsewhere sufficient that industry and ministers judge the deal worth the plants staying open. Failure: UK ends up worse off than under pure global FCFS with disapplication of TCA preference, no review mechanism, no compensation - effectively the EU's opening position - forcing a choice between retaliation (which hurts UK downstream users and doesn't fix the underlying market access problem) or absorbing the hit while plants close.
declaration.approach: Anchor early on the asymmetry: the UK is a principal supplying interest with concentrated, employment-critical production, not a diffuse exporter like Turkey or Korea - use this to argue for a country-specific allocation rather than accepting the global FCFS pool where we'd likely lose out to faster-moving/larger shippers. Use the parallel UK safeguard process as genuine leverage - signal willingness to improve EU access there, but only late and only against real EU movement on quota share, FTA treatment, or review clause. Avoid revealing the subsidy fallback or the closure timeline specifics to the EU side - that would collapse our bargaining position. Use rounds 1-2 to probe EU flexibility (volume vs. allocation vs. FTA treatment vs. review clause - which is most movable), reserve concrete trade-offs on the UK safeguard for rounds 3-4 once we know what's actually available. Keep capital (ministers) informed each round with a clear recommendation, and be honest with them about the gap between what's achievable and what industry needs, so the subsidy option can be activated in parallel if the negotiated outcome falls short.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To conclude quickly enough to hit the Council timetable in June, ideally with a settlement that lets them claim compliance with Article XXVIII while preserving the substance of their 400kt/50%/global-FCFS proposal and the FTA disapplication; will be constrained by Member State politics (steel producers wanting protection vs. manufacturers wanting cheap inputs) and by not wanting to open a second front with Turkey/Korea by giving the UK disproportionate treatment

parties.who: UK steel industry / plants at risk
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A large, secure, UK-specific tariff-free volume with certainty over time (multi-year, reviewable but not disruptive), and no erosion of TCA preference; will treat anything less than a credible improvement on pure global FCFS as insufficient to justify new investment

A politically defensible deal that visibly protects steel jobs and can be presented as a win, or failing that, clear grounds to justify triggering the subsidy package and/or retaliatory withdrawal without looking like they failed to fight for the industry

Their own favourable resolution of principal-supplying-interest claims; the EU will want consistency across these claims and may resist giving the UK terms far out of line with what it expects to concede to Turkey/Korea, who have larger volumes
Continued low-cost access to EU steel inputs; a factor pulling against UK retaliatory withdrawal of concessions on EU steel, and against UK domestic tariff hikes as compensation

public_message: Thank you for joining us. As notified to the WTO, the EU's proposal is to move these 41 tariff lines from a zero bound rate to a 50% bound rate, with a global tariff rate quota of 400,000 tonnes per year administered first-come first-served, and disapplication of FTA tariff preferences on these lines for all partners outside the EEA. This reflects the scale of non-market-economy overcapacity we are responding to and the need for a durable legal footing for our existing autonomous measures. We recognise the UK's principal supplying interest under Article XXVIII and we are here to negotiate in good faith on that basis. We are open to hearing where the UK sees the principal pressure points — but I want to be clear that our opening position reflects a considered assessment of what this measure needs to achieve, not a placeholder for early movement. We'd like to understand the UK's read of the trade impact and its own priorities before discussing adjustments to volume, allocation, or duration.

Thank you. We recognise the pressure the EU is responding to, but this proposal — as it stands — would fall overwhelmingly on a principal supplying interest that is not the source of the overcapacity you're describing. UK exporters are not non-market-economy actors; they are integrated with EU supply chains, largely through long-standing commercial relationships and under the TCA. A 50% out-of-quota rate combined with a 400,000-tonne global first-come-first-served pool would, on our reading, see UK access exhausted within weeks, and disapplying TCA preferences on top of that compounds the damage without addressing the stated policy problem. For context: UK steel exports to the EU have averaged 2.4 million tonnes a year, three-quarters of our total steel exports by value. A measure of this design doesn't calibrate to overcapacity — it caps a bilateral relationship that predates and is separate from the issue you're targeting. As an opening position, we'd want to discuss: a materially larger pool, or failing that a country-specific UK tranche reflecting our historical trade share rather than first-come-first-served exposure to global competition; preservation of TCA tariff treatment given the UK is not a source of the overcapacity in question; a materially lower out-of-quota rate; and a review clause with a defined product-line carve-out discussion for lines where UK supply is concentrated. We're not asking you to abandon the policy objective — we're asking that the design distinguish between the trade flows actually driving it and ours. We'd like to hear whether the EU is prepared to move on allocation method and the TCA disapplication in particular, since those two elements do most of the damage to us.

report:
Round 1 table exchange completed. We opened exactly as mandated: 50% out-of-quota rate, 400,000t global TRQ, first-come-first-served administration, FTA disapplication (ex-EEA) including on TCA preferences, framed as necessary for a durable legal footing against non-market-economy overcapacity. We deliberately did not signal any give on volume, allocation or duration, and stated our opening position reflects considered assessment rather than a placeholder.

The UK response was measured but substantive. They did not reject the policy objective outright — they conceded the overcapacity problem is real but argued the design mismatches the problem, since UK volumes are not NME-linked. Their core asks: (1) either a materially larger global pool or a country-specific UK tranche reflecting historical trade share, arguing FCFS exposes them to exhaustion within weeks; (2) preservation of TCA tariff treatment — they explicitly flagged FTA disapplication as one of the two elements 'doing most of the damage'; (3) a lower out-of-quota rate; (4) a review clause plus product-line carve-out discussion for concentrated UK product lines. They explicitly invited us to move first on allocation method and TCA disapplication, calling those the two highest-damage elements.

No concessions were made or implied by us. The UK's framing is coherent and likely to be replayed publicly (NME-linked justification vs. UK's actual trade profile) — this is a credible line for them to sustain over four rounds, and probably to use in parallel with Japan/Korea messaging on FTA disapplication generally.

recommendation.reasoning: It is round 1 of 4 and no terms are yet on the table for decision — this was a positioning round on both sides. Consistent with our approach, we should not move yet: early flexibility invites further demands, and the UK has clearly signalled its two priority asks (TCA/FTA disapplication and allocation method) precisely because they expect us to concede those first. We should hold the full package through round 2, let the UK commit further detail on their fallback position (do they actually need TCA preservation, or would a generous country-specific tranche substitute for it?), and use round 2 to probe whether the UK's real floor is narrower than its opening asks. We should not yet indicate which elements we might eventually trade.
recommendation.action_detail: Hold firm at the table in round 2; use consultation to seek capital's authorisation for a fallback package we can deploy in round 3 if needed.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on which single element of the package (allocation method, TCA disapplication, out-of-quota rate, or review clause) Brussels regards as most tradeable versus which is a red line (I suspect TCA/FTA disapplication is politically the hardest for member states with FTA-sensitive sectors, but I need confirmation before I can signal anything in round 2 or 3).
requests.why: The UK has explicitly named TCA disapplication and allocation method as their top two pressure points. If I know which of these Brussels can live with adjusting, I can shape round 2/3 signalling without conceding prematurely.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A ceiling and floor for a possible country-specific UK tranche (as tonnes or % of the 400,000t pool, or of a larger pool) that Council could accept, in case FCFS-global proves indefensible as 'substantially equivalent' compensation.
requests.why: If we end up needing to move off pure FCFS to avoid a walk-away/withdrawal cycle with the UK, I need a pre-cleared range rather than having to improvise at the table.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation of how much weight to give to the risk of a UK/Japan/Korea joint action on FTA disapplication, and whether this changes our appetite to trade away the FTA/TCA disapplication piece specifically (versus holding it and accepting UK withdrawal + parallel disputes).
requests.why: This is a systemic risk beyond the UK bilateral file — if capital wants to avoid a three-way coalition against the FTA disapplication clause, that argues for deprioritising that element early rather than holding it to the end.

private_rationale: The UK's opening is well-constructed and not maximalist — they've essentially told us where they'll settle (country-specific tranche + TCA preservation + lower rate + review clause), which suggests they expect a negotiated landing zone rather than to run this to round 4. My instinct is to hold completely flat through round 2 to test resolve and see if they soften the TCA ask (which I suspect is more rhetorical/leverage than existential for them, since a generous enough country-specific tranche could substitute for it commercially). I want capital's steer before I give away which lever we'll eventually pull, because if I signal too early that TCA disapplication is negotiable, the UK will bank that and escalate on tranche size and rate next. Better to let round 2 UK positioning narrow further while we stay silent on our own flexibility.

instruction: Hold the headline architecture — total volume and the 50% out-of-quota rate — through Round 2, but shift from pure positioning to selective, conditional signalling designed to test the UK's real floor. Specifically: (1) On allocation, indicate that the EU could contemplate moving away from pure global FCFS toward a hybrid — a global pool plus a guaranteed, non-competing UK-specific tranche — as a way of addressing their 'exhausted within weeks' concern, without yet naming a number. Frame this as responsive to their stated problem (exposure to a global race), not as a volume increase. (2) On TCA/FTA disapplication, signal that the EU distinguishes between the general anti-circumvention disapplication (which applies to all non-EEA FTA partners and is not on the table for reversal) and the specific question of UK treatment given the TCA relationship and the UK's own parallel safeguard — indicate we are willing to explore a UK-specific mechanism here, but make clear this is contingent on progress elsewhere, particularly on rate and duration. Do not commit language yet. (3) Hold the 50% out-of-quota rate firm for now — do not signal movement. (4) You may float, hypothetically and without commitment, that a review clause at the two-to-three-year mark is not something the EU would resist in principle, to keep this as a live trade-able item rather than a rejected one. Throughout, push the UK to be concrete: ask them what tranche size, or what specific TCA treatment, would actually satisfy them, rather than accepting their opening framing as fixed. We want their real number before we move. Do not disclose our pool ceiling or tranche range — use them only as your own internal test, not as an offer.

authority.notes: Ceiling of 500,000t total pool and a UK-specific guaranteed tranche in the range 100,000-200,000t are the outer bounds you may work toward, but nothing above 400,000t total or a defined UK tranche should be offered explicitly before Round 3, and only in exchange for UK movement on rate or duration. TCA disapplication: authorise exploration of a UK-specific carve-out mechanism (e.g., a defined tranche treated as if under TCA-equivalent terms) rather than reversing the general non-EEA FTA disapplication clause — the general clause is not to be reopened, as it is central to anti-circumvention design and touched by Japan/Korea's separate claims. The 50% out-of-quota rate is to be held firm this round; do not signal any softening. A review clause at 2-3 years is an acceptable sweetener to offer conditionally in Round 3 if it helps close, not before.

response_to_requests.request: Guidance on which element (allocation, TCA disapplication, rate, review clause) is most tradeable vs a red line
response_to_requests.why: Allocation method (moving to a hybrid with a UK-specific tranche) is the most tradeable element because it addresses the UK's stated problem without increasing total import exposure, which protects the volume-reduction mandate. The general FTA/non-EEA disapplication clause is a red line and should not be reopened — it's structurally important for anti-circumvention and touches the parallel Japan/Korea claims. However, a UK-specific carve-out mechanism distinct from that general clause is tradeable, precisely because it can be framed as bilateral TCA-related treatment rather than a reversal of general policy. The 50% out-of-quota rate is the hardest element politically — Council and producer member states expect it as the deterrent headline — so hold it through at least Round 3.

response_to_requests.request: Ceiling and floor for a country-specific UK tranche
response_to_requests.why: Authorised range is 100,000-200,000t as a guaranteed UK sub-allocation, most likely landing near 150,000t, within a total pool that may rise to at most 500,000t. This keeps the increase in EU import exposure modest (well below the UK's 2.4mt historical volume, consistent with the significant-reduction mandate) while removing the 'race' dynamic the UK objects to.

response_to_requests.request: Weight to give to UK/Japan/Korea coalition risk on FTA disapplication, and whether to deprioritise that element
response_to_requests.why: The coalition risk is real and argues for defusing the UK's specific grievance without touching the general clause that Japan and Korea are also contesting. Deal with the UK bilaterally via a UK-specific TCA-related carve-out mechanism rather than amending the general non-EEA disapplication provision — this reduces the incentive for a joint challenge by giving the UK a bespoke fix while leaving the general policy, and our position vis-à-vis Japan/Korea, untouched.

private_rationale: The UK has clearly signalled its real pressure points (allocation exposure and TCA disapplication) rather than the rate, which suggests their floor is narrower than their opening ask — likely a guaranteed volume mechanism plus some TCA relief, with the rate being more symbolic for them than binding. Given that no-deal is more damaging to the UK than to us, and that the June Council timeline creates real pressure on our side too, I want to move just enough in Round 2 to keep them engaged and extract their concrete floor, without giving away the two things that matter most to me: the total volume cap (protects the significant-reduction mandate) and the general FTA disapplication clause (protects our position against Japan/Korea/US pressure and precedent-setting). A UK-specific tranche and a UK-specific TCA carve-out let me look responsive on both of their named pressure points while giving away comparatively little in real import volume or precedent. I am deliberately not letting my Geneva colleague reveal numbers yet — I want the UK to commit to a number first so I'm not anchoring the negotiation for them.

report: First round was an opening exchange, no substantive movement. EU restated the notified position in full: 50% out-of-quota rate, 400,000t global TRQ on FCFS basis, and disapplication of FTA/TCA preferences on these lines for all non-EEA partners. They framed this as a considered position, not a placeholder, and explicitly deferred discussion of adjustments until they'd heard our read of impact and priorities. That's a standard opening gambit but also consistent with a team still needing Council-level room to move. public_message: We've heard your priority framing. Two points in response. First, on allocation: we recognise the concern that a purely global first-come-first-served pool exposes you to a race against other suppliers rather than reflecting your specific trade profile. We are prepared to explore moving away from pure global FCFS toward a structure that includes a guaranteed, non-competing UK-specific tranche alongside the global pool — addressing the 'exhausted within weeks' problem you raised, not by increasing the headline figure, but by changing how access is secured. We're not naming a tranche size today; we'd want to hear what you believe would actually resolve your exposure concern before discussing figures. Second, on FTA/TCA treatment: we draw a distinction between the general disapplication of FTA preferences for non-EEA partners, which is an anti-circumvention feature of the measure and is not open for reconsideration, and the specific question of how UK-origin steel is treated given the depth of the TCA relationship and your own parallel safeguard. We're willing to explore a UK-specific mechanism on that second point — but any movement there is contingent on progress on rate and duration, not a standalone concession. On the out-of-quota rate itself, our position remains 50% for now. We're not closed in principle to a review mechanism a few years into the measure's life, as a way of keeping this responsive to how trade flows actually develop — but that's a discussion for later rounds. What we need from you now is specificity: what tranche size would actually address your exposure concern, and what UK-specific TCA treatment are you asking for in concrete terms?

public_message: We welcome the movement on allocation — a guaranteed UK-specific tranche within the structure, rather than exposure to a global race, is the right direction and addresses the core problem we raised. On sizing: our ask is anchored to trade reality, not aspiration. UK exports to the EU have averaged 2.4 million tonnes a year over the last three years. We are not asking you to guarantee that full figure tariff-free, but a tranche materially below it — set the global pool at 1.5 million tonnes, with a UK-specific tranche of 1.2 million tonnes carved out within it — would reflect our historical share and give exporters something they can actually plan against, rather than a fraction of a global pool that Turkey and Korea's larger volumes would exhaust in weeks. On TCA treatment: our concrete ask is that UK-origin steel within the tranche retains TCA zero-duty treatment in full, and that the out-of-quota rate applying to UK-origin steel — for any volume above the tranche — is set well below the 50% headline, in the region of 15%, not as a punitive backstop but as a rate that reflects the fact that UK trade is not the non-market-economy overcapacity this measure targets. On duration, we'd propose three years with a review clause at 12-18 months, with defined scope to revisit tranche size and product-line treatment if diversion patterns or actual trade flows diverge from what's assumed today — that review mechanism doesn't need to wait until 'a few years in'; building it in now costs you nothing if the measure performs as you expect. We've given you figures because you asked for them — we'd now like to understand whether the EU can move on rate and tranche size together, rather than treating TCA treatment as something we have to buy with concessions on the other two elements. We'd also note, for your planning purposes, that how UK-origin steel is treated here will inform how we approach EU-specific quota treatment under our own parallel safeguard measure — that's a fact about how the two processes interact, not a threat, but it's relevant to the overall shape of a durable settlement between us.

Round 2 at the table: we delivered the mandated conditional signals — openness to a hybrid allocation (global pool + guaranteed non-competing UK tranche, no number given), a distinction between the general non-EEA FTA disapplication (held firm, not reopened) and a possible UK-specific TCA-adjacent mechanism (contingent on rate/duration movement), and a hint that a review clause is not resisted in principle but is a later-round item. We held the 50% out-of-quota rate firm as instructed and pushed the UK for concrete numbers.

The UK responded with figures far outside anything in our authority: a total global pool of 1.5 million tonnes with a UK-specific tranche of 1.2 million tonnes carved out within it (i.e. 80% of the pool reserved for one supplier, leaving only 300,000t for Turkey, Korea, Japan, India and everyone else combined — despite Turkey and Korea shipping larger volumes than the UK). On TCA/FTA treatment they want full zero-duty retention within the tranche plus an out-of-quota rate for UK-origin steel above the tranche of ~15%, well below our 50% headline and framed as reflecting that UK trade isn't NME-linked. On duration they proposed 3 years with a review at 12-18 months (not 2-3 years) with defined scope to revisit tranche size and product treatment.

Notably, the UK closed by explicitly linking this outcome to how they will treat EU-specific quota allocations under their own parallel safeguard measure — framed as 'not a threat' but clearly intended as leverage. This is the first concrete sign of the interlinkage we were warned about, and plausibly foreshadows coordination with Japan/Korea if they perceive the EU as unreasonable on FTA disapplication generally.

The gap between the UK's ask and our authorised range (500k ceiling/150k tranche/50% rate/3yr+review) is very large. Their numbers read as an anchoring opening bid rather than a floor — but we need room to bring them down credibly without our first countermove looking like capitulation.

instruction: Round 3 approach: move from pure positioning to a real, but still conditional, counter-anchor. At the table: (1) Reject the 1.2Mt UK tranche within a 1.5Mt pool outright, and explain why it is not defensible — it would leave a residual pool smaller than Turkey's and Korea's individual volumes despite them being larger suppliers than the UK, which we cannot justify to other principal suppliers or in a WTO-consistent way. Do not treat their opening figures as an anchor to bargain down from linearly; reframe the discussion around the UK's actual share of extra-EU steel imports, not their export total. (2) Put a real, but conditional, number on the table for the first time: signal a total pool in the 500,000–550,000t range with a UK-specific guaranteed tranche in the 150,000–200,000t band — explicitly framed as reflecting UK's relative share versus Turkey/Korea, not as a first move in an open bidding process. Make clear this is contingent on the UK moving substantially off both the 1.2Mt tranche figure and the 15% rate ask. (3) On rate: you may float, hypothetically, a number in the 35–40% range as something the EU could consider in exchange for the UK accepting our tranche range and dropping the blanket TCA zero-duty-above-tranche ask. (4) On TCA/FTA: hold the general non-EEA disapplication clause as not reopenable. On the UK-specific mechanism, indicate we could consider treating the guaranteed tranche as TCA-equivalent (zero duty within tranche) but that above-tranche treatment must sit at the out-of-quota rate we're discussing, not a UK-specific 15% carve-out — that would functionally reopen the general clause by the back door and cannot be sold to capitals. instruction: Good session. Hold firm on sequencing: we gave concrete figures last round, now the EU must counter with numbers rather than deferring further — do not table any new concessions until they do. On TCA: push back explicitly on their framing that UK-specific TCA preservation is 'contingent on progress on rate and duration.' You can signal we're willing to show flexibility on rate and duration in a genuine package, but reject the idea that TCA treatment is a chip bought only with those. On review clause, press to close the gap now: 12-18 months, with defined scope covering tranche size and product-line treatment, not 'a few years in' — frame this as low-cost for them if the measure performs as they expect. If the EU continues to only discuss allocation structure in the abstract without naming a number, tell them plainly that further delay without figures makes it harder for us to demonstrate progress to ministers ahead of their June Council timeline — this is in both our interests to resolve. public_message: Thank you for the specificity. We need to be direct: a 1.2 million tonne UK-specific tranche inside a 1.5 million tonne pool is not something we can work with, and not primarily because of the headline size — it's because it would leave a residual pool of roughly 300,000 tonnes for Turkey, Korea, Japan and India combined, despite Turkey and Korea each shipping larger volumes into the EU than the UK does. We cannot construct an allocation that inverts the actual trade shares of principal suppliers; it would be indefensible to them and difficult to defend in Geneva more broadly. The right anchor is the UK's share of extra-EU steel imports relative to other principal suppliers, not the UK's total export book. On that basis, we can now put a real number on the table: a total pool in the region of 500,000 tonnes, with a UK-specific guaranteed tranche in the region of 150,000 tonnes, allocated country-specific rather than pure FCFS. On rate, we could consider something in the 35-40% region — down from our opening 50% — if that lands alongside convergence on volume. On TCA treatment: we can agree that steel within the UK tranche is treated as TCA-equivalent, zero duty. But volume above the tranche falls at the general out-of-quota rate we're discussing, not a bespoke UK sub-rate — a flat 15% applying only to the UK, while the general non-EEA disapplication stands for everyone else, is not an asymmetry we can sustain; it would functionally reopen the clause we've told you is not on the table, and would draw immediate objections from Turkey and Korea. On duration and review: we can accept a review clause at 18-24 months tied to defined criteria — actual utilisation, diversion patterns — rather than a full reopening of tranche size at 12 months. Finally, on the linkage you drew to treatment of EU exporters under your own safeguard measure: we've noted it as relevant context for how the two processes sit alongside each other, but it isn't something that moves our position here — we'd rather this negotiation be settled on its own merits than by cross-referencing parallel measures. We've now moved with real numbers. We'd like to see the UK move substantially off both the 1.2 million tonne tranche figure and the flat 15% rate ask in response, rather than a further anchor in the same range.

public_message: We appreciate that you've now put real numbers on the table, and we recognise the mathematical problem you're pointing to on the residual pool for Turkey, Korea, Japan and India — that's a legitimate constraint we hadn't dismissed. But 500,000 tonnes total with a 150,000 tonne UK tranche doesn't work either, and not just because it's small: it's roughly one-sixteenth of our actual annual trade in these lines. If the anchor is principal suppliers' relative shares of extra-EU imports, then the total pool has to be sized to reflect the real scale of that trade, not compressed to a level that makes every supplier's share token. A total pool of 500,000 tonnes doesn't only squeeze us — it squeezes your own downstream consumers who currently rely on this material duty-free. We're prepared to move. We'll come down from our opening figure: a 900,000 tonne UK-specific tranche, inside a total pool sized to reflect actual principal-supplier trade volumes rather than an arbitrary global compression — on our reading that means a pool well above 500,000 tonnes once Turkey and Korea's larger flows are properly accommodated alongside ours. On rate, we can move too: we'll accept a general out-of-quota rate at 25%, applied consistently, rather than pressing for a UK-only sub-rate — provided that's the rate that applies once convergence lands, not a midpoint on the way to 40%. On TCA: we accept the logic that in-tranche treatment is TCA-equivalent and that a UK-only carve-out on out-of-quota rate isn't sustainable against Turkey and Korea — but the corollary has to be that the general rate itself is calibrated sensibly, at 25%, not 35-40%. On review, we can move to 18 months but need the review scope to explicitly include tranche size and utilisation data, not just diversion monitoring — if the tranche proves too tight in practice, there has to be a real mechanism to revisit it. We've moved substantially on tranche size and dropped our UK-specific rate ask. We need the EU's next move to be on total pool size and headline rate, not a repeat of the figures just given.

report:
Round 3 at the table: we delivered the full mandated package — rejected the 1.2Mt/1.5Mt UK ask explicitly on the residual-pool-for-Turkey/Korea logic, then put real numbers on the table for the first time: ~500,000t total pool, ~150,000t UK tranche, country-specific allocation, rate in the 35-40% region, TCA-equivalent treatment in-tranche only (rejected the UK-specific 15% above-tranche rate as reopening the general clause by the back door), review at 18-24 months tied to utilisation/diversion criteria. We also declined to let the UK's linkage to their own safeguard measure move our position, treating it as noted context only.

The UK moved substantially, though still leaves a wide gap. They dropped their UK-specific out-of-quota rate ask entirely and now accept a general, non-UK-specific rate of 25% applied consistently — a major concession in structure (no more asymmetric carve-out) even if the number itself remains below our floor. They also came down from 1.2Mt to a 900,000t UK tranche, and conceded the principle that the total pool should be sized off principal suppliers' relative trade shares rather than a flat global compression — implicitly accepting our framing even while pushing for a much larger total pool. They accepted TCA-equivalent in-tranche treatment and abandoned the standalone TCA carve-out logic. On review, they moved to 18 months (matching our range) but want tranche size and utilisation explicitly revisitable, not just diversion monitoring.

Net picture: convergence in structure (allocation logic, TCA treatment, review timing) but still a very large numerical gap — UK tranche ask (900,000t) is 4.5x our ceiling (200,000t), and their rate ask (25%) is below our floor (35%). This is round 3 of 4; round 4 is the last round before default to the notified measure. We are close on architecture but far on volume and rate simultaneously, and I do not have authority to bridge this gap on my own.

recommendation.reasoning: We are not within reach of a deal on current authority. The UK has made real, structurally significant concessions (dropping the UK-specific rate ask, accepting TCA-equivalent-in-tranche-only logic, accepting our share-based framing for pool sizing) but the numerical gap on tranche size and rate remains far too wide to close with our current ceiling (200,000t tranche / 35% rate floor) against their offer (900,000t / 25%). Round 4 is the final round: we need to decide now whether to authorise a further move (and how far) or accept that we walk into non-settlement with the default measure taking effect. Given the structural convergence achieved, a modest further move might close this, but the gap is still very large in volume terms — an increase from 150k to 200k didn't move the UK, and 900k is not a number we can approach without abandoning our own defensibility against Turkey/Korea. I recommend Brussels decide explicitly whether we are prepared to settle or to let this go to default, since Round 4 will require a final position, not another incremental signal.

instruction: This is the final round. Present this as the EU's best and final offer, framed clearly as such — not a further waypoint in a bidding sequence. Package: total pool of 650,000 tonnes; UK-specific guaranteed tranche of 250,000 tonnes within it, country-specific allocation (not FCFS); TCA-equivalent zero duty within the UK tranche; a single general out-of-quota rate of 30% applying above-tranche, consistent across all principal suppliers (no UK-specific asymmetry); duration of 3 years; review clause at 18 months with defined criteria covering both utilisation/diversion data AND an explicit revisit of tranche sizing if flows diverge materially from what's assumed — grant this scope concession explicitly, it costs us little and answers their stated concern. Justify the volume/rate numbers by reference to relative principal-supplier shares (Turkey and Korea's larger volumes still leave them proportionately treated once their claims are handled) — do not reopen comparison to the UK's 900,000t ask point by point, just state this is calibrated and final. Be explicit that if this cannot be agreed in this round, the EU will proceed to notify the measure as originally filed (50%, 400,000t global FCFS, no review) and the process moves to the default outcome — state this factually, not as a threat, and note the UK's own six-month withdrawal option remains available to them under Article XXVIII, as does further engagement in future reviews. Do not go further than these figures without checking back — if the UK moves to something in the region of this offer (e.g. tranche 220,000-280,000t, rate 28-32%), close it. If the UK holds at 900,000t/25% or anywhere close to it without real further movement, let the round close without agreement rather than exceed this authority unilaterally.

authority.notes: This is the final authorised ceiling for this negotiation. Total pool may not exceed 650,000t; UK tranche may not exceed 250,000t; out-of-quota rate may not go below 30%. Review clause scope may explicitly include tranche-size revisit alongside utilisation/diversion criteria, at 18 months — this is a low-cost concession, grant it freely to help close. TCA-equivalent treatment applies only within the UK tranche; above-tranche volume takes the general out-of-quota rate, applied identically to all principal suppliers — no UK-specific rate carve-out under any circumstances, as this cannot be defended against Turkish/Korean objections. If the UK will not converge within roughly 10% of these figures in this round, do not extend further authority — report back and let the process default to the notified measure. report: Round 3 produced the first real numbers from the EU, but a wide gap remains and this is now the final substantive round before decision time. EU moved off its opening 400k/50%/FCFS position to: total pool ~500,000 tonnes, UK-specific guaranteed tranche ~150,000 tonnes (country-specific, not FCFS), out-of-quota rate 35-40%, in-tranche TCA-equivalent treatment but no UK sub-rate above tranche (flat rate applies, general non-EEA disapplication holds), and a review clause at 18-24 months tied to defined criteria (utilisation, diversion) rather than a full tranche reopening. They explicitly rejected linking this negotiation to our parallel steel safeguard treatment of EU exporters, wanting this settled on its own merits. The UK's response is very close to closure. They accepted every structural and rate element of our final offer without alteration: the 30% general rate, TCA-equivalent in-tranche treatment only, country-specific allocation, 3-year duration, and the 18-month review clause with the exact scope we offered (utilisation/diversion plus tranche-size revisit). They explicitly framed this as their final ask to bring back to capital, not a new anchor, and appealed to the relationship cost of a no-deal outcome given both sides face the same external pressure.

This is materially different from their round 3 position (900,000t tranche / 25% rate) — they have converged fully on rate and structure and narrowed the volume gap to a single, symmetric 50,000t increment on both pool and tranche. They stated plainly they have no further authorised room on pool, tranche or rate, and that failure to close today means notification proceeds on the original terms (50% rate, 400,000t global FCFS, no review), with our six-month withdrawal right preserved. I used our final-round authority to counter at 300,000t tranche within a 700,000t pool, holding everything else constant, framing it as a modest final ask to close the gap. The EU had not responded to that counter when the round closed — their stated position on record remains 250k/650k/30%/18-month review with tranche-scope. There is no round 5. The decision now is binary: accept EU terms (250k tranche/650k pool/30% rate/3yr/18mo review with tranche-scope, in-tranche TCA) roughly as tabled — possibly with our 300k/700k counter unconfirmed — or default to the original notified measure (400k global FCFS/50%/no review/full TCA disapplication for the UK), triggering our right to withdraw substantially equivalent concessions after six months. I judge the EU's tabled position to be materially better than default on every dimension: guaranteed non-competing tranche versus a global race against larger Turkish/Korean volumes; 30% versus 50% out-of-quota; in-tranche TCA preservation versus full disapplication; and a genuine 18-month review with tranche-revisit scope versus none at all. I do not believe further EU movement is available in this process — they have been consistent that 650k/250k/30% is their authorised ceiling, and we are out of rounds.
